title: America’s Loneliness Epidemic Just Got Worse. For the Diaspora, It Never Really Got Better.
excerpt: A new APA survey finds 42 per cent of Americans experience loneliness at least once a week — up from 33 per cent last year. For South Asians living thousands of miles from family, the numbers are only part of the story.
body:
The number was already grim. Now it is worse.

In 2025, one in three Americans said they experienced loneliness at least once a week. In 2026, that number has jumped to 42 per cent. One in six — 16 per cent — say they feel lonely every single day. The data, from the American Psychiatric Association’s annual Mental Health Survey of more than 2,200 adults, paints a picture of a country that is collectively anxious, increasingly isolated, and running out of easy fixes.

The economy tops the list of anxieties: 71 per cent of respondents said they were very or somewhat anxious about it. The Iran war (63 per cent), healthcare (62 per cent), and gun violence (62 per cent) followed close behind. Nearly half — 48 per cent — said they were more anxious than the year before.

And there is a new worry climbing the charts. Anxiety about artificial intelligence surged from 44 per cent in 2025 to 53 per cent in 2026, a nine-point jump that suggests the unease around AI is no longer confined to tech circles.

When Loneliness Becomes a Health Crisis

The surgeon general’s 2023 advisory was blunt: chronic loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. A study of 600,000 people published in Nature Mental Health found that feeling isolated raises the risk of dementia by 31 per cent. The stress hormone cortisol, which rises with sustained loneliness, is a known accelerant of heart disease, stroke, and cognitive decline.

The coping mechanisms people reach for are telling. The two most common responses to loneliness, each at 54 per cent, are watching TV and listening to music — activities that are passive, solitary, and unlikely to build the human connections that loneliness demands.

Meanwhile, 65 per cent of Americans said they had never spoken to a healthcare professional about their mental health. The stigma may be easing — 60 per cent said mental illness is less stigmatised than a decade ago — but the gap between acknowledging a problem and actually seeking help remains vast.

“Americans are telling us that anxiety remains a part of daily life, coming from many directions at once, including financial pressures, safety concerns, and rapid technological change,” said Marketa M. Wills, the APA’s CEO and Medical Director.

The Diaspora’s Quiet Crisis

For South Asians living in the United States, the loneliness data carries a particular sting. This is a community built around family density — joint families, daily phone calls, festivals celebrated in crowds. Migration strips much of that away. The uncle who dropped by unannounced, the neighbour who brought over extra rotis, the grandmother who was always, structurally, present — these are not features you can replicate on a WhatsApp video call.

The “model minority” framework compounds the problem. South Asian professionals are expected to be thriving — successful careers, good schools for the kids, a house in the suburbs. Admitting to loneliness can feel like admitting to failure, particularly in a culture where mental health conversations are still met with discomfort. The data on South Asian mental health utilisation consistently shows that this community is among the least likely to seek professional help.

First-generation immigrants face the sharpest version. Their English may be strong enough for work but not for the kind of casual, layered social interaction that builds genuine friendship. Their cultural references do not land. Their food smells different in the office microwave. These are small things, individually. They are not small things, cumulatively.

Second-generation South Asians face a different flavour of the same problem: code-switching between two worlds, fully at home in neither, navigating parents who do not understand their social landscape and friends who do not understand their family obligations.

What Actually Helps

The research is clear on what does not help: more screen time, more passive consumption, more isolation dressed up as introversion. What works is structured, in-person social contact — even low-stakes interaction like a weekly trivia night, a gym class, or a standing lunch with a colleague.

Former surgeon general Vivek Murthy, himself the child of Indian immigrants, has been touring the country advocating for social connection as a public health priority. “To help someone else feel less alone, to help them feel seen and understood and valued,” he told KFF Health News, “that can be one of the most powerful interventions that we make.”

For the diaspora, this is not abstract public policy. It is the question of whether the life you built abroad has room for the connections that made the life you left behind worth living.

The APA’s numbers say America is getting lonelier. For a community that crossed oceans and left behind the architecture of belonging, the question is not whether loneliness exists. It is whether anyone is willing to talk about it.
